title: The Cognitive Revolution
note: Harari argues that around 70,000 years ago Sapiens gained the ability to share stories about things that do not exist, which let large groups of strangers cooperate. Treat this as his thesis: the dates, Dunbar's number and megafauna extinctions are empirical, and scholars debate how sudden the change was.

read.title: Stories that scale
text: Harari argues that the key to Homo sapiens success is not strength or tools but a kind of talk. Around 70,000 years ago, he says, Sapiens developed a flexible language that could describe things nobody could see or touch: spirits, tribes, laws, companies. He calls such things imagined realities, and says they exist in the shared minds of many people, which he labels intersubjective.

Why does that matter? His argument draws on a figure from anthropologist Robin Dunbar, who linked primate brain size to group size and suggested that people can keep close track of about 150 others. Gossip, Harari says, helps a band of that size hold together. Beyond that size, he argues, you need shared stories so that strangers will cooperate. A company, a nation or a religion works because enough people believe in it.

This is an interpretation, not a settled finding. Dunbar's number is a rough estimate, and a 2021 analysis found that the underlying brain data support a wide range of values. Many archaeologists also see symbolic behavior in Africa building up slowly rather than appearing in one jump 70,000 years ago.

The extinctions of large animals in Australia and the Americas are empirical. Harari ties them mainly to human hunters. Most scholars grant humans a role, but climate change is also debated as a cause.

q.q: What is Dunbar's number, according to the reading?
o: About 150 people one can keep track of

q.q: According to Harari, what lets strangers cooperate in large groups?
Why does the reading call the Cognitive Revolution an interpretation?
o: Many archaeologists see a gradual change instead of a sudden jump
